newsitem.title: CHINA: Wife demands medical treatment for China dissident.
newsitem.headline: Wife demands medical treatment for China dissident.

text.p: The wife of jailed dissident Liu Nianchun has demanded that Chinese authorities allow her ailing husband to seek medical treatment, a New York-based human rights watchdog group said on Thursday.

Chu Hailan wrote to the head of parliament and Beijing's mayor on March 8, threatening to stage a sit-down demonstration if authorities did not let her husband see a doctor before the end of the month, Human Rights In China said.
"I do not wish to see the illness of my husband worsen because of delays in medical treatment," Chu said in her letter, a copy of which was made available to Reuters by the group.
"If this happens, I will take all legitimate means, including litigation, demonstration, sit-down protest...to protect the rights of my husband," she said.
Chu said her husband, imprisoned in the Shuanghe labour camp in northeast China, suffered from intestinal problems, an enlarged lymph node and ulcers in his mouth.
Chinese officials reached by telephone declined to comment.

In July, authorities ordered Liu to serve three years of re-education through labour for drafting a petition that urged the government to free all political prisoners and reassess its 1989 crackdown on student demonstrators in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Re-education through labour is a form of administrative punishment that can be imposed by authorities without a trial.
Liu appealed the labour camp term, but Beijing's Chaoyang District Court rejected the motion last December.

Western human rights activists say re-education through labour is increasingly favoured by authorities as a way of removing dissidents from circulation without the complications and publicity of a trial.

Liu was editor of a magazine during the Democracy Wall movement in the early 1980s and was sentenced in 1981 to three years in prison for spreading counter-revolutionary propaganda and for incitement, or subversion.
In its annual report on human rights, the U.S. State Department accused Beijing of effectively silencing public dissent in 1996 through jailings, intimidation or exile.
The Hong Kong-based Information Centre of Human Rights and Democratic Movement in China said 42 pro-democracy activists were jailed in 1996.
China dismisses criticism of its human rights record as interference in its internal affairs.
